strengths: Novel training-free defense: The paper presents an elegant test-time mitigation strategy that leverages cyclic measurement consistency with synthesized sampling patterns, avoiding costly retraining while preserving reconstruction fidelity on clean, unperturbed inputs.

Rigorous theoretical grounding: Theorem 1 and its detailed proof in Appendix G clearly explain the mechanism of error propagation in algorithm-unrolled networks, formally showing why input perturbations on acquired k-space locations disproportionately corrupt the unacquired frequency coordinates.

Physically meaningful attack modeling: In addition to standard standard lp attacks, the paper connects adversarial vulnerability to practical MRI phenomena such as impulse noise leading to herringbone artifacts, establishing a valuable bridge between adversarial machine learning and clinical MRI physics.

Thorough evaluation against adaptive attacks: Following best practices in adversarial robustness, the authors evaluate the defense against white-box adaptive attacks (unrolling the defense for up to 100 steps) and rigorously verify that gradient obfuscation is avoided.

Generality across architectures and setups: The approach demonstrates strong quantitative and qualitative gains across multiple distinct unrolled network architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, E2E-VarNet, Recurrent-VarNet), non-uniform sampling masks, and in blind mitigation scenarios.
weaknesses: Test-time computational latency: Because the mitigation requires iterative reverse PGD passes—each involving multi-coil forward/backward operators and neural network evaluations across K masks—the inference runtime is substantially increased compared to standard forward reconstruction. A detailed wall-clock timing analysis and discussion of real-time clinical feasibility would strengthen the practical impact.

Sensitivity to synthetic noise level: The cyclic consistency objective introduces a synthesized noise term to match measurement SNR. A more systematic ablation on the sensitivity of the mitigation to noise variance mismatch or noise estimation errors is desirable.

Reporting of statistical variability: In Table 1, Table 2, and Table 3, results are presented as aggregate mean metrics without standard deviations or statistical significance tests across test subjects/slices.

strengths: Novel and elegant physics-driven formulation: The paper leverages cyclic measurement consistency across synthesized undersampling patterns to formulate a test-time, training-free defense (via reverse PGD) that searches for a corrective perturbation within an epsilon-ball without requiring model retraining.

Rigorous robustness and adaptive attack evaluation: Defenses often suffer from false security due to obfuscated gradients. The authors explicitly construct white-box adaptive attacks by unrolling the mitigation procedure and backpropagating through it, systematically verifying criteria (such as iterative vs. single-step attack strength and perturbation scaling) to ensure true robustness.

Broad empirical validation across models and data: The proposed defense is evaluated on multiple architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, E2E-VarNet, Recurrent-VarNet), two fastMRI datasets (knee and brain), and under different undersampling trajectories, consistently restoring high visual and quantitative quality.

Practical considerations and artifact modeling: Connecting adversarial vulnerabilities to clinically observed herringbone artifacts (sparse impulse noise in k-space modeled as an l0 perturbation) and introducing a blind parameter search procedure provide meaningful practical relevance.

Solid theoretical motivation: Theorem 1 provides an analytical upper bound on the error on acquired k-space locations, formally explaining why adversarial degradations inevitably propagate into unacquired k-space lines and why cycle consistency exposes them.
weaknesses: Inference computational overhead: Because the defense relies on an iterative test-time optimization (reverse PGD) passing through deep unrolled networks multiple times over K synthesized masks, test-time latency is significantly increased compared to standard forward reconstruction or adversarially trained models. Explicit wall-clock runtime comparisons should be documented in the main text.

Computational cost in blind mitigation: The linear scheduling heuristic used to jointly search for epsilon and alpha requires running optimization loops sequentially, multiplying test-time computation and potentially hindering real-time clinical deployment.

Clarification on Theorem 1 interpretation: Theorem 1 establishes that ||E_Omega (x~ - x)||_2 <= C ||w||_2. The deduction that ||E_Omega^C (x~ - x)||_2 must be large relies on the prerequisite that the adversary successfully produced a large total image distortion ||x~ - x||_2. Making this explicit in the text would strengthen the mathematical presentation.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated formulation: The core insight—that data fidelity forces adversarial errors into the unacquired frequency support (Omega^c), which can be exposed and corrected via cyclic measurement consistency with resampled patterns—is elegant, physically grounded, and novel for adversarial defense in deep learning inverse problems.

Theoretical support: Theorem 1 provides an analytical error propagation bound over acquired frequencies versus unacquired frequencies in unrolled networks, offering a clear theoretical foundation for why cyclic consistency across complementary k-space trajectories detects and mitigates perturbations.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The method is evaluated across two benchmark datasets (fastMRI knee Cor-PD and brain Ax-FLAIR), five distinct unrolled architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, E2E-VarNet, Recurrent-VarNet), multiple perturbation types (image-domain l_infinity, k-space l_2, and l_0 herringbone impulse noise), and both uniform and non-uniform sampling masks.

Rigorous evaluation against adaptive attacks: Following robust defense evaluation best practices (Athalye et al., 2018; Tramer et al., 2020), the authors evaluate adaptive white-box adversaries by unrolling the mitigation graph (up to T=100) and explicitly verifying that defense effectiveness is not an artifact of gradient obfuscation.

Training-free and preservation of clean data: Unlike adversarial retraining methods that suffer from clean performance degradation and heavy retraining compute, the proposed test-time mitigation preserves clean reconstruction fidelity and converges immediately on clean inputs.
weaknesses: Inference-time computational latency: While the approach eliminates model retraining, the test-time reverse PGD optimization (Algorithm 1) requires evaluating the unrolled network multiple times across K synthesized sampling patterns for tens to over a hundred iterations. The manuscript lacks explicit wall-clock runtime measurements and memory benchmarks, which are critical considerations for clinical deployment and real-time scanning pipelines.

Assumptions underlying theoretical bounds: The error propagation bound in Theorem 1 relies on Lipschitz bounds on the proximal neural network and smooth coil sensitivity maps. In unconstrained unrolled models without explicit Lipschitz regularization (e.g., spectral normalization), the Lipschitz constant can be large, potentially loosening the bound.

Evaluation limited to standard distortion metrics: Quantitative evaluation relies almost exclusively on PSNR and SSIM. In clinical MRI, adversarial perturbations can produce subtle anatomical hallucinations or obscure micro-pathologies (such as fine tears or lesions), which are not always reliably reflected by global pixel-level metrics.

strengths: Original and well-motivated framework: The paper introduces a test-time, training-free adversarial defense for physics-driven deep learning (PD-DL) MRI reconstruction based on cyclic measurement consistency, avoiding the costly retraining and clean-data performance degradation associated with adversarial training.

Solid theoretical foundation: Theorem 3.1 establishes that data fidelity in unrolled networks bounds output errors on the acquired k-space indices while forcing adversarial perturbations into the unacquired frequency complement, providing rigorous mathematical backing for the cyclic consistency mechanism.

Extensive and rigorous evaluation: The method is validated across multiple datasets (fastMRI knee and brain), multiple unrolled architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, E2E-VarNet, Recurrent-VarNet), and various attack formulations (ell_infty, ell_2, and a domain-specific sparse ell_0 model for herringbone artifacts).

Careful treatment of adaptive attacks and gradient obfuscation: Following best practices from the adversarial robustness literature, the authors properly evaluate the defense against fully adaptive white-box adversaries via unrolled gradient backpropagation and verify the absence of gradient obfuscation.

Comprehensive experimental extensions: The paper thoughtfully investigates blind mitigation (unknown perturbation size), compatibility with pre-existing robust training strategies, comparisons with classical input transformations and diffusion purification, as well as generalization to dynamic MRI and image inpainting.
weaknesses: Test-time computational and memory overhead: Mitigating attacks requires multi-step iterative optimization with gradient backpropagation through unrolled neural networks, increasing per-slice reconstruction time from fractions of a second to several seconds (and requiring substantial GPU memory, up to ~21-66 GB), which could be a bottleneck in high-throughput clinical workflows.

Heuristic nature of synthesized sampling masks: The generation of cyclic sampling masks relies on shifting equispaced masks or random patterns sharing ACS lines; a deeper analysis of sensitivity to synthetic mask selection for non-Cartesian or arbitrary irregular sampling patterns is somewhat limited.

strengths: Principled and novel formulation: The paper cleverly leverages cyclic measurement consistency with synthesized sampling patterns to design a test-time, training-free mitigation strategy specifically tailored to physics-driven deep learning (PD-DL) inverse problems.

Rigorous theoretical justification: Theorem 3.1 and Appendix D provide a formal error propagation analysis demonstrating why adversarial perturbations on acquired frequencies leak primarily into the unacquired frequency complement, directly explaining why cyclic resampling exposes and corrects the perturbation.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: The authors evaluate across multiple datasets (fastMRI knee, brain, dynamic cardiac cine), various unrolled architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, VarNet variants), and multiple baselines (adversarial training, SMUG, randomized smoothing, TV, JPEG, and diffusion purification).

Adherence to robustness best practices: The paper thoroughly investigates adaptive attacks by unrolling the defense and backpropagating through the computational graph, explicitly verifying the absence of gradient obfuscation according to established criteria.

Broad practical scope: The authors connect adversarial models to real-world MRI acquisition issues (herringbone artifacts modeled as sparse impulse noise) and show successful performance in blind settings where attack strength and type are unknown.
weaknesses: High inference latency and memory requirements: Because mitigation requires iterative gradient descent with multiple forward/backward passes through unrolled networks, inference time increases by over two orders of magnitude (~6.78 seconds per slice vs. ~0.04 seconds for baseline inference) and requires substantial GPU memory (21.3 GB for 2D, 66.5 GB for dynamic MRI), which may hinder deployment in high-throughput or real-time clinical settings.

Scope restricted to physics-driven architectures: The theoretical guarantee and practical efficacy rely fundamentally on the presence of explicit data fidelity operations that enforce measurement consistency on acquired frequencies. Consequently, the defense cannot directly protect purely image-to-image architectures lacking physics-based consistency layers.

Stopping criteria details: In Algorithm 1, the termination condition ('until Converge') in the iterative setting is left somewhat vague in the main text; providing precise stopping tolerances or iteration bounds in the main algorithm box would improve immediate reproducibility.

strengths: Novel and conceptually sound formulation: The paper cleverly exploits cyclic measurement consistency across synthesized undersampling patterns to detect and mitigate adversarial perturbations at test-time without requiring model retraining.

Strong theoretical support: Theorem 3.1 and the detailed error propagation analysis in Appendix D provide rigorous justification for why perturbations on acquired k-space lines \(\Omega\) primarily distort the unacquired complement \(\Omega^c\), explaining the effectiveness of cyclic measurement consistency.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across multiple public datasets (fastMRI knee Cor-PD, brain Ax-FLAIR), multiple architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, E2E-VarNet, Recurrent-VarNet), various perturbation types (\(\ell_\infty\), \(\ell_2\), and \(\ell_0\) herringbone spikes), and against competitive baselines (Adversarial Training, SMUG, randomized smoothing, TV, diffusion purification).

Rigorous evaluation against adaptive attacks: The authors explicitly evaluate adaptive attacks by unrolling and backpropagating through the defense objective (up to \(T=100\) steps) and verify against standard gradient obfuscation sanity checks (Athalye et al., 2018), showing that iterative cyclic mitigation remains resilient.

Practical clinical connection: Modeling k-space impulse spikes (herringbone artifacts) as a sparse \(\ell_0\)-bounded adversarial attack connects theoretical adversarial vulnerability to real-world scanner hardware anomalies.
weaknesses: Inference latency and memory footprint: Because mitigation requires solving an iterative reverse PGD optimization involving multiple forward/backward passes through unrolled networks, inference time increases from ~0.04s to 6.78s per slice, and peak memory reaches 21.3 GB (up to 66.5 GB for dynamic MRI). This could limit high-throughput clinical workflows.

Strict dependence on physics-driven unrolled architectures: The cyclic consistency mechanism relies on explicit data fidelity projection at acquired lines \(\Omega\). As noted in Appendix M, it cannot be directly applied to black-box image-to-image neural network architectures that lack forward-operator consistency.

Heuristic nature of blind parameter tuning: While the blind mitigation scheme (Appendix G) demonstrates empirical success, optimizing \((\epsilon, \alpha)\) using linear decay schedules relies on empirical convergence heuristics without theoretical convergence guarantees.
